slot.brief: For a sparingly soluble salt of a given dissolution equation (e.g. with 2:1 stoichiometry), relate solubility s to Ksp, then compute either s from Ksp or Ksp from s; also compare solubilities of two salts with same/different stoichiometry.

stem: The solubility products of two sparingly soluble salts, $\text{MX}$ and $\text{NY}_2$, are $4.0 \times 10^{-10}$ and $3.2 \times 10^{-11}$, respectively, at $298\ \text{K}$. The ratio of the molar solubility of $\text{NY}_2$ to that of $\text{MX}$ in water is:
working:
For the salt $\text{MX}$:
$$\text{MX}(s) \rightleftharpoons \text{M}^+(aq) + \text{X}^-(aq)$$
If the molar solubility is $s_1$, then:
$$K_{\text{sp}}(\text{MX}) = [\text{M}^+][\text{X}^-] = s_1^2$$
$$s_1 = \sqrt{4.0 \times 10^{-10}} = 2.0 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$$

For the salt $\text{NY}_2$:
$$\text{NY}_2(s) \rightleftharpoons \text{N}^{2+}(aq) + 2\text{Y}^-(aq)$$
If the molar solubility is $s_2$, then:
$$[\text{N}^{2+}] = s_2, \quad [\text{Y}^-] = 2s_2$$
$$K_{\text{sp}}(\text{NY}_2) = [\text{N}^{2+}][\text{Y}^-]^2 = s_2(2s_2)^2 = 4s_2^3$$
$$s_2 = \left(\dfrac{3.2 \times 10^{-11}}{4}\right)^{1/3} = \left(8.0 \times 10^{-12}\right)^{1/3} = 2.0 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$$

The ratio of the solubility of $\text{NY}_2$ to that of $\text{MX}$ is:
$$\dfrac{s(\text{NY}_2)}{s(\text{MX})} = \dfrac{2.0 \times 10^{-4}}{2.0 \times 10^{-5}} = 10$$

Independent check: MX: Ksp=s², s=√(4.0×10⁻¹⁰)=2×10⁻⁵ M. NY₂: Ksp=4s³=3.2×10⁻¹¹ → s³=8×10⁻¹² → s=2×10⁻⁴ M. Ratio s(NY₂)/s(MX)=2×10⁻⁴/2×10⁻⁵=10.
